Shreya had heard the story of the missed train three times now, and it kept changing. In January, over pani puri at the colony market, her friend Sonali had said Aakash forgot to book the tickets. In March, it was Sonali who "must have forgotten to remind him". Tonight, on Shreya's balcony in Pune, Sonali said, "Honestly, I think I got the date wrong. Aakash says I always mix things up."
Shreya remembered the screenshot Sonali had sent her that January morning: Aakash's own message saying he would book them. She didn't pull it up. She only asked, "Have you noticed that in every version, you end up the confused one?"
Sonali laughed, then stopped, and looked down into her tea. "He's usually right, though."
"Maybe," Shreya said. "I just remember it differently. I'm here whenever you want to compare notes."

qa.q: Where was Sonali when she told the story in January?
qa.a: She was at the colony market, over pani puri.

qa.q: What does Sonali's laugh that suddenly stops suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Shreya's question touched something true; Sonali may be starting to feel uneasy about always being the confused one, even while defending Aakash.

qa.q: Why was Shreya's choice not to pull up the screenshot a wise one?
qa.a: Showing proof might have felt like an attack and made Sonali defend Aakash harder; a gentle question and an open offer to compare notes lets Sonali see the pattern herself.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sonali to hear that every version ends with her confused?
qa.a: It may be unsettling and a little embarrassing, because it challenges her belief that Aakash is usually right, but it also gives her an outside anchor for her memory.

grounding: A friend hears the same missed-train story shift over months until Sonali is always the confused one, and gently points out the pattern.

"So Sam says the anniversary dinner fight was my fault," Noor said, stirring her coffee in the office pantry. "I was too loud at the restaurant."
"Wait," Divyansh said. "Last week you told me Sam walked out because you ordered dessert."
"Did I? Maybe. Sam says I remember things dramatically."
"Noor, can I say something as your friend, and you can tell me to shut up?"
"Go."
"That's the fourth fight you've told me about since June. Every time, the story changes when you retell it, and every time, the last version is that you got it wrong."
Noor put the spoon down. "That's just because I think about it more later."
"Could be. I'm not inside it, so I don't know. I'm only noticing the shape from out here."
"The shape."
"Same shape. Every time."
Noor was quiet. "Can I tell you the next one as soon as it happens? Before I think about it?"
"Anytime."

qa.q: Where does the conversation take place?
qa.a: It takes place in the office pantry, over coffee.

qa.q: Why did Noor put the spoon down?
qa.a: Noor was struck and a little uneasy as Divyansh's point, that every story ends with her being wrong, started to land.

qa.q: What did Divyansh's approach get right?
qa.a: Divyansh admitted not knowing what happens inside and pointed only to the repeated shape, which let Noor listen without feeling attacked or judged.

qa.q: What might it be like for Noor to see the pattern Divyansh describes?
qa.a: It could be frightening and confusing, since it suggests her own sense of events has been worn down, but her request to share the next fight straight away shows she wants an outside anchor.

grounding: A friend who has heard four fights retold notices each one ends with Noor being wrong, and names the pattern without claiming to know the inside story.

passage:
I'm Parul, and Salma has been my closest friend since college. For a year, we've had chai every Sunday, and every Sunday she tells me about a fight with her husband.
The strange thing is how the stories go. In March she said he shouted at her for visiting her mother. By April, retelling the same day, she said she'd "provoked" him. In June, a new fight: he'd forgotten her birthday, and by the end of the story, she was the one apologising for "making a big deal."
Every story ends the same way. He's right. She's confused.
Last Sunday she said, "I think I'm just bad at remembering things." And I felt cold all over. Salma remembers every birthday of every cousin.
I didn't argue. I said, "Can I tell you what I've noticed? Every time, the story flips, and you end up the one who's wrong. I'm worried about you." She stared at her cup for a long time.

qa.q: What did Salma's husband forget in June?
qa.a: He'd forgotten her birthday.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when Salma said she was bad at remembering things?
qa.a: Parul felt cold all over and worried, because Parul knew Salma remembers every cousin's birthday and saw the pattern clearly.

qa.q: What did Parul do that could help Salma?
qa.a: Parul gently described the noticed pattern without arguing, and said she was worried, leaving Salma room to think.

qa.q: How might Salma feel hearing Parul's observation?
qa.a: Salma may feel shaken and confused, but also seen, which is why she stares at her cup for a long time.

grounding: It shows a friend hearing the same fights retold with the partner always right and the teller always confused, and seeing the pattern first.

Team lead's note, Friday. Something I want to remember about Avni.
Over the last two months, Farida has told the team several stories about her fiancé at lunch. I noticed, and so did Avni, that each story changes shape as it goes. It begins with something he did. It ends with Farida saying she "overreacted," or "must have misunderstood," or "is too emotional."
Most of the team just nodded. Avni didn't. After lunch today, I saw her walk with Farida to the lift. I heard her say quietly, "I've noticed that in every story, you end up the one who's wrong. I might be off. But I'm worried, and I'm here if you want to talk."
Farida laughed it off at first. Then she said, "Can we get coffee on Monday?"
Avni came to my desk afterwards, looking shaken. I told her she'd done the right thing, and gave her the number of our employee counselling service to pass on.

qa.q: How does each of Farida's stories end?
qa.a: It ends with Farida saying she "overreacted," or "must have misunderstood," or "is too emotional."

qa.q: How did Avni seem to feel after talking to Farida?
qa.a: Avni seemed shaken and worried, having named a painful pattern gently to someone she cares about.

qa.q: What did Avni do that fits a wise response?
qa.a: She named the pattern gently, admitted she might be wrong, offered to be there, and the team lead gave her the counselling number to pass on.

qa.q: How might Farida feel after Avni's words?
qa.a: Farida may feel uncomfortable at first, laughing it off, but also cared for enough to ask for coffee on Monday.

grounding: A team lead records a colleague noticing that a friend's stories always end with her wrong and confused, and gently naming the pattern.

Tuesday night
Harish came over again tonight, and I listened to another story about Megha. I've started writing them down, because I think something is wrong.
In January, he said Megha screamed at him in a restaurant. By February, retelling it, he said he'd "embarrassed her first." Tonight he described her deleting his photos with his friends, and by the end he said, "I probably deserved it. I get things mixed up."
My little brother used to be the sharpest person I know. Now he says "I'm confused" in every conversation about her.
I've read my notes three times. The pattern is so clear from outside: every story starts with something she did and ends with him apologising.
I'm scared of pushing him away. But tomorrow I'm going to tell him, gently, what I've noticed, and give him the name of the counsellor my friend saw.
Charu

qa.q: What did Harish say Megha deleted?
qa.a: His photos with his friends.

qa.q: What is Charu feeling as she writes?
qa.a: Charu feels worried and scared, both for Harish and of pushing him away by saying what she has noticed.

qa.q: What does Charu plan to do tomorrow?
qa.a: Charu plans to tell Harish gently what she has noticed and give him the name of a counsellor.

qa.q: How does Harish seem to see the fights now?
qa.a: Harish seems confused and blames himself, saying he probably deserved it and gets things mixed up.

grounding: A diary notices a younger brother's stories always flip to him being wrong and confused, seeing the pattern before he does.
